opus-5.5.text:
I think the difference really starts with what each community believes the core problem is.

For a lot of traditional robotics researchers — and I'd include myself in that lineage, since I came up through manipulation and control — the instinct is to decompose. You have perception, state estimation, planning, control, and you try to make each module correct and understandable. There's a strong culture of rigor: you want guarantees, you want to know why the robot did what it did, and when it fails you want to point to the module that broke. That mindset produced a lot of beautiful work, especially in locomotion and structured industrial settings. But it tends to struggle with the long tail of the real world: deformable objects, clutter, novel tools, all the messy contact-rich stuff where writing down the right model is basically impossible.

Large-model researchers come at it from almost the opposite direction. Their prior is: don't hand-design the structure, get the data and the scale right, and let the model figure out the representation. They've seen that work in language and vision, so the natural question is, can we treat robot actions as just another modality and train a big policy end to end? That brings real strengths: generalization across tasks, the ability to use internet-scale pretraining for semantic understanding, and a willingness to iterate fast and empirically rather than waiting for a clean theory.

Where it gets interesting is that each side underestimates something. Large-model people sometimes underestimate how different robot data is. There's no internet of robot actions. Data is expensive, embodiment-specific, and the physical world doesn't forgive mistakes the way a chatbot conversation does. Latency, safety, and contact dynamics matter a lot. Traditional roboticists, on the other hand, sometimes underestimate how far scale and good data can take you, and how much of what we thought needed explicit modeling can just be learned if the data distribution covers it.

So my view is that the most productive path is a kind of synthesis. Take the large-model lesson seriously: invest in data, in scalable data collection systems, in general-purpose policies. But keep the roboticist's respect for the physical world: good hardware, good low-level control, careful thinking about what data actually teaches the policy. A lot of my own work has been about that intersection: how do you design hardware and data collection so that the data you get is actually high-quality and transferable, instead of just a lot of it.

And honestly, I think the gap between the two communities is closing fast. Students now are fluent in both languages. Five years from now, I suspect the distinction will feel a bit artificial. We'll just be people trying to build robots that work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions scalable data collection and respect for the physical world, but does not contrast those with traditional researchers inspecting the physical circumstances of individual data points.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that large-model researchers rethink what information robots need because they are less habituated to existing robot perception systems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that the two groups start from opposite ends of the same problem and have very different instincts about where the hard part lives.

Traditional robotics people come from a world where the robot is the object of study. You think about kinematics, dynamics, control loops, contact, friction, latency. You decompose the problem: perception, planning, control, each as its own module with clear interfaces. The culture is engineering-first, very bottom-up. When something fails, you want to know exactly which module failed and why, and you fix that piece. There's a deep respect for the physical world, because the physical world has punished you many times. You know that a sim-to-real gap of a few millimeters can break everything, that a gripper slipping is not a modeling error you can wave away.

Large-model people come in with a completely different prior. Their formative experience is that scale plus data plus a simple objective beat hand-engineered structure, over and over, in language and vision. So their instinct is to say, don't decompose. Treat the robot as another modality. Feed it pixels and proprioception, output actions, and let the model figure out the structure internally. They care about data pipelines, pretraining, generalization across tasks, and they tend to be comfortable with the system being a black box as long as the aggregate behavior improves. Their question isn't "which module failed," it's "do we have enough data of the right kind, and is the model big enough."

Where it gets interesting is what each side underestimates. The model people often underestimate how expensive real-world data is and how unforgiving physics is. In language you can scrape the internet; in robotics every sample costs real time on real hardware, and the long tail of failures is physical, not statistical. The robotics people, on the other hand, often underestimated how much of what they carefully engineered could be learned, and how brittle their modular pipelines were once you left the lab. A lot of classical stacks worked beautifully on exactly the setting they were built for and fell apart one room over.

What I see now is a convergence, but not a symmetric one. The end-to-end, foundation-model framing has clearly become the center of gravity. But the people doing the best work are the ones who import the robotics discipline into it: careful attention to data quality, to hardware, to evaluation in the real world rather than benchmarks, to the fact that a 95% success rate is a failed product. So the question is less "which camp is right" and more "how do you build a team that holds both intuitions at once," because either one alone will get stuck.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model researchers’ interest in data pipelines and data volume with robotics researchers’ attention to physical constraints, but it does not say that one group focuses on scaling collection while the other inspects the physical circumstances of individual data points.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect large-model researchers’ willingness to rethink what information a robot needs to being less accustomed to existing robot perception systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is where they expect the intelligence to come from. Traditional robotics researchers tend to start with the physical system: its dynamics, its sensors, its actuators, and the constraints it has to operate under. They break the problem into perception, planning, and control, and try to make each part reliable. Large-model researchers tend to start with learning: can we collect enough data and train a model that acquires useful behaviors across many tasks?

That leads to different instincts when something fails. A roboticist might ask whether the state estimate is wrong or the controller needs improving. A large-model researcher might ask whether the training data covers that situation or whether the model can generalize better. Those are tendencies, of course; there’s plenty of overlap.

The interesting challenge is bringing the two together. A model can give a robot broader understanding, but physical interaction demands precise timing and feedback. Understanding an instruction like “pick up the cup” is one problem; adjusting your grip when the cup starts slipping is another. I think progress comes from combining the breadth of learned models with the discipline robotics has developed around acting reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says large-model researchers may collect enough data to train useful behaviors, but it does not contrast that with traditional researchers inspecting the physical circumstances of individual data points.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that large-model researchers rethink what information robots need because they are less habituated to existing perception systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is where they expect the robot’s capabilities to come from. Traditional robotics researchers tend to start with the physical system: its mechanics, sensors, control, and the constraints of a particular task. They break the problem into parts—perception, planning, control—and try to make each part reliable and understandable.

Large-model researchers tend to start with learning: can we collect enough data and train a sufficiently general model so that many of those capabilities emerge together? Instead of designing a separate solution for every task, they look for a shared representation that can transfer across tasks and environments.

Those starting points also shape how they react to failure. A roboticist might ask, ‘Is the calibration wrong? Is the controller unstable?’ A large-model researcher might ask, ‘Is this situation missing from the training data? Do we need a different training objective?’ Both are useful questions.

For me, the interesting opportunity is bringing them together. A robot has to generalize, but it also has to act reliably in the physical world. Learning can broaden what it can do, while robotics gives us the tools to understand and constrain how it does it.

r001.rationale: The response says large-model researchers seek enough training data, but it does not contrast this with traditional researchers inspecting the physical circumstances of individual data points.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that large-model researchers are more willing to rethink what information a robot needs because they are less accustomed to existing perception systems.
